clinicalPearls: Defined by the combination of a hypothalamic hamartoma with central (mesoaxial) or postaxial polydactyly
Hypothalamic hamartomas may cause gelastic (laughing) seizures, central precocious puberty or hypopituitarism
A bifid or partially cleft epiglottis is a highly suggestive, if under-recognised, feature
Other findings include imperforate anus, renal anomalies and, occasionally, laryngotracheal clefts
Caused by heterozygous truncating GLI3 variants, typically in the middle third of the gene, with autosomal dominant inheritance
Allelic with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly, which results from a different position or class of GLI3 variant
GLI3 acts downstream of hedgehog signalling processed at the primary cilium, linking the disorder to ciliary biology
reference.pathophysiology: Pallister-Hall syndrome results from heterozygous truncating variants in GLI3, typically in the middle third of the gene, that generate a shortened protein biased towards its transcriptional repressor form. GLI3 is the principal transcriptional effector of hedgehog signalling, a pathway that is assembled and processed on the primary cilium, so the disorder is intimately linked to ciliary biology. During development the resulting imbalance of hedgehog output disturbs patterning of the hypothalamus, limbs, larynx and hindgut, producing the hypothalamic hamartoma, central or postaxial polydactyly, bifid epiglottis and anorectal and renal anomalies. The contrasting effect of GLI3 loss-of-function variants elsewhere in the gene explains why Greig cephalopolysyndactyly is allelic yet clinically distinct.
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to identify and characterise a hypothalamic hamartoma
Endocrine evaluation for precocious puberty and anterior pituitary function
Radiographs of the hands and feet to document central or postaxial polydactyly
Laryngoscopy for bifid epiglottis and airway assessment where indicated
Examination and imaging for imperforate anus and renal anomalies
redFlags: Gelastic seizures or intractable epilepsy arising from the hamartoma
Panhypopituitarism, which can be life-threatening in the neonate through adrenal insufficiency
reference.prognosis: With recognition and management of endocrine and airway problems the outlook is generally good and intellect is usually normal; the hypothalamic hamartoma is benign and malformative, though associated seizures can be difficult to control.
pitfalls: Missing neonatal hypopituitarism and adrenal insufficiency, which can be fatal
Attempting resection of a hypothalamic hamartoma without recognising its benign, malformative nature
Overlooking a bifid epiglottis on airway assessment
Confusing it with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly despite the shared GLI3 basis
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Anti-seizure medication for gelastic and other seizures arising from the hypothalamic hamartoma, with stereotactic laser ablation or surgical disconnection for refractory epilepsy
Endocrine hormone replacement for hypopituitarism and a GnRH analogue to manage central precocious puberty
Airway assessment and surgical repair of a bifid epiglottis or laryngotracheal cleft where symptomatic
Surgical correction of imperforate anus and evaluation and management of renal anomalies
Orthopaedic or plastic surgical review for central or postaxial polydactyly
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant GLI3 inheritance and family testing
Coordinated multidisciplinary care across neurology, endocrinology, ENT, surgery and clinical genetics
